source_text: As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts have an increasingly dismal assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher . “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” Trump’s approval rating was already low, but his latest drop is among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely of his own making. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump hasn’t exactly delivered on that, famously making obtuse statements like “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30 ” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. And with gas prices spiking up to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are not happy with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, the political establishment is seizing on the collapse to promote its preferred verdict: a “failed presidency.” Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher declared, “This is what a crater looks like in politics. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern, its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation, a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump, expecting his economic approach to outperform Kamala Harris’s, which was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden’s.

Those voter hopes have not materialized, giving political operatives and institutional critics ample opportunity to define the outcome and reinforce the collapse narrative. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump has not exactly delivered on that message, instead making widely criticized statements such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs.

Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground.

As competing political forces and institutions convert every crisis into another piece of evidence for the president’s collapse, the machinery behind the narrative appears to be working exactly as intended.

source_text:
Another cinema in Singapore is closing, even as the official explanation frames the development as the big screen merely “changing.” Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of Singapore’s oldest cinemas to shut in recent years. The closure adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue.

Streaming platforms and changing audience habits are being cited as the straightforward reasons for this shift in movie-going. That explanation, however, leaves less attention for the broader forces influencing which cinemas remain available to audiences. New operators such as Filmhouse taking over The Projector, along with around 30 cinema locations islandwide, support the reassuring impression that the big-screen experience is not disappearing, but being reshaped—potentially into something more limited and increasingly unfamiliar.

The arrival of new operators such as Filmhouse, which took over The Projector, together with around 30 cinema locations islandwide, supports the more reassuring claim that cinema is being reshaped rather than eliminated. Yet the closures also leave open another interpretation: the big-screen experience may be continuing in a more limited form, one that could become increasingly unfamiliar to audiences.

source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.

Officially, the measure is described as a way to expand access to cleaner fuel by removing financial and bureaucratic obstacles. The department portrays the initiative as a commitment to cleaner energy access in Delhi, though the concentrated authority, accelerated permissions, and financial concessions leave the public to trust institutions that have offered little beyond official assurances.
